teaching_blocks.title: Define the Prediction Task
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine an operations team wants an estimate before deciding which delivery orders need attention. ‘Predict a late delivery’ sounds clear until two engineers use different decision times or different meanings of late. A task record makes those choices explicit before you prepare examples.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Define the prediction problem in terms of the inference to be generated and the example data needed to support it. Inputs for a prediction must be information available at its prediction time, not information that only becomes available afterward. An empirical outcome proportion is the count of that outcome divided by the total count in the specified population; a conditional outcome proportion uses only the count in its specified conditioning group.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Write the task record with one prediction unit, a target event or value, the time a prediction is made and the horizon over which the target is judged, so the example/target relationship is unambiguous.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this invented task, one prediction unit is an order at acceptance. The target event is arrival more than 30 minutes after acceptance, judged over that 30-minute horizon. Distance and the promised delivery zone are available at acceptance; the eventual arrival time is not an input. Suppose a supplied population contains 100 orders, of which 20 meet the target event. Its empirical outcome proportion is 20/100 = 0.20. Within a specified zone, 12 of 40 orders meet it, giving a conditional proportion of 12/40 = 0.30. The denominators answer different questions: all orders versus orders in that zone. Record both the population and the horizon beside the counts so another engineer can interpret the same task.

Notice how changing the prediction unit would change the task. If the unit were a whole delivery zone rather than an individual accepted order, neither the input row nor the target event in this fixture would be the same. Similarly, a horizon of one hour would ask a different question from the stated 30 minutes. Keep unit, decision time, target and horizon in separate record fields so those changes cannot masquerade as implementation details. When reporting 0.30 for the zone, say which zone and which eligible orders provided the denominator. The task definition establishes the interpretation that subsequent dataset and model work must preserve.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A target is not interchangeable with an input. The later arrival can establish whether this example met the target, but cannot become information supplied to a prediction made at acceptance. Nor does the zone proportion describe every zone.

video_need.reason: A timeline and a small count table help connect decision time, target horizon and the two conditioning populations.

teaching_blocks.title: Numerical Arrays for ML
teaching_blocks.content: Your prediction fixture declares two features per order. Before doing any arithmetic, you need to distinguish three observations with two features from one flat collection of six values. Array rank and axis lengths make that distinction inspectable.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Create an array from the supplied list or tuple fixture with import numpy as np and np.array(fixture); inspect its ndim, shape and dtype. For a declared two-axis batch/feature contract, check a.ndim == 2 and compare a.shape[1] to the declared feature count before accepting the input. The shape tuple gives the length of each axis, so the batch-length requirement can be checked with a.shape[0] after checking rank.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Reject a violated input requirement with a conditional raise ValueError(message), rather than continuing with an invalid array. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Consider the fixture [[2, 10], [4, 20], [6, 30]]. The declared interpretation is three orders and two features per order, so rank 2, shape (3, 2), and feature width 2 satisfy the contract. A fixture [2, 10, 4, 20, 6, 30] contains the same number of values but has rank 1, so it fails this contract. Check rank before looking for a second axis. A rank-2 fixture with shape (3, 1) fails the feature-width rule instead. Include an accepted fixture, a declared batch-length boundary and a rejected fixture in the checks. When a production input violates the rule, raise the declared ValueError instead of allowing the later operation to decide what the input meant.

Read the shape from left to right under the declared interpretation: the first length counts observations, and the second counts features within each observation. This tells you where to check batch boundaries and where to check model input width. Do not index shape[1] before establishing rank 2; a flat failure fixture does not have that second axis. Dtype is another independent contract field. An array can have the accepted shape while using the wrong numerical representation, or the accepted dtype while having the wrong axes. Keep those failures distinguishable in tests so fixing one check does not accidentally waive another.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Total element count does not establish the meaning of the axes. Also, an assert is a fixture check during ordinary non-optimized execution, not an unconditional substitute for explicit input rejection.

teaching_blocks.title: Numerical Arrays for ML
teaching_blocks.content: An order feature matrix must fit a numerical storage budget, but a smaller representation is useful only if it preserves values well enough for the declared task. Inspect both the values and the bytes rather than selecting a dtype from its name alone.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A numerical dtype specifies a representable value range and a bit width, so candidate integer and floating types need not preserve the same input values. Inspect a.dtype and explicitly cast with a.astype(candidate_dtype) when comparing representations. For a fixed-width numerical array, a.size × a.itemsize is its element-storage byte count, exposed by a.nbytes; it excludes non-element object overhead.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the cast values with the reference values using arithmetic differences before accepting a lower-precision representation; casting can overflow or lose precision.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a reference fixture contains six values and you are comparing fixed-width representations with element widths of eight and four bytes. Their element-storage totals are 6 × 8 = 48 bytes and 6 × 4 = 24 bytes. That comparison says nothing about other object overhead. Explicitly cast the reference into the candidate representation, inspect the candidate dtype and subtract reference values to reveal changes. For instance, if a supplied candidate represents a reference value 1.25 as 1.0, the difference is −0.25. Whether that is acceptable depends on the fixture's declared tolerance; the byte saving does not decide it. Keep the reference values available while checking the candidate, so the comparison is not between two copies of the already altered values.

Inspect a value near a declared precision or range boundary as well as ordinary values. The purpose is to expose the candidate conversion's actual difference from the retained reference, not to assume that every smaller dtype behaves badly or that every successful cast is acceptable. Compare the difference using the fixture's explicit tolerance. A zero difference on one ordinary value is not enough to waive the remaining declared fixtures. Also keep the number of elements unchanged when comparing element bytes; otherwise a reduced total could come from fewer observations instead of a narrower representation. The choice balances measured preservation with the specified storage budget.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Fewer bytes is not the same as a faithful representation. A cast can lose precision or overflow, and array.nbytes is element storage rather than the whole memory cost of using the array.

teaching_blocks.title: Numerical Arrays for ML
teaching_blocks.content: You want to subtract one reference value for each of two order features across three observations. Array arithmetic can express that operation without a Python operation written separately for every observation, but the axes still determine what gets combined.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: NumPy arithmetic operations can operate elementwise on arrays instead of executing a Python operation once per observation. Broadcasting compares axes from the right; aligned lengths must be equal or one must be 1, and missing leading axes are treated as length 1. Check the resulting shape as well as operand compatibility, because compatible broadcasting can expand the result to a larger shape.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Use np.testing.assert_allclose(array_result, reference_result, rtol=..., atol=...) to test agreement with the list-comprehension reference under explicit tolerances.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For the invented matrix [[2, 10], [4, 20], [6, 30]], subtract [1, 5]. The trailing feature lengths match, so the result is [[1, 5], [3, 15], [5, 25]], with shape (3, 2). Verify it against a list-comprehension reference using explicit tolerances. Now compare operands shaped (3, 1) and (1, 2): compatible broadcasting yields a (3, 2) result, not a (3, 1) result. If the contract expected one output per observation without an extra feature axis, compatibility alone would not make that result acceptable. Write the intended result shape beside the numerical reference, and check both instead of accepting an operation simply because it completed.

Work through one output row to check meaning as well as compatibility. The first row [2, 10] minus the two feature references [1, 5] becomes [1, 5]. The same reference is then applied to each later observation. A reference operation should express that intended per-feature rule, not simply duplicate an accidental broadcast. For the (3, 1) and (1, 2) case, expanding three row positions against two column positions creates six outputs. That is why validating the output shape matters even when no exception was raised. The check ties the succinct operation to a concrete result rather than treating compact syntax as correctness.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Broadcasting is not permission to combine arbitrary axes. Right-aligned compatibility and the resulting shape are separate checks; a compatible operation can still produce a larger result than intended.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Vectorization operates over axes; broadcasting aligns compatible dimensions.

teaching_blocks.title: Ingest and Inspect Model Data
teaching_blocks.content: The platform supplies an authorized storage location and a dataset contract. Your job is to retrieve the intended existing object and verify the loaded representation, not create a new storage platform or assume the first object in a listing is the right dataset.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: With an authorized Google Cloud Storage client, client.list_blobs(bucket_name, prefix=prefix) iterates existing objects matching the supplied prefix. Select the intended object by name and use bucket.blob(object_name).download_to_filename(local_path) to obtain a local dataset file. Read a CSV with pd.read_csv(local_path, dtype=declared_types), and verify its loaded columns, row count and value representations against the expected dataset.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: CSV is a delimited text format, while Parquet is a columnar format whose reader can select columns; choose the supplied format according to the required access pattern. Use with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") as f for a local text identity record, and use f.read() or f.write(text) within the block. Import the Google Cloud Storage dependency with from google.cloud import storage and construct storage.Client() using the existing authorized runtime identity.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Import pandas as pd and apply explicit per-column conversions for the declared types, inspecting the converted values rather than accepting inference as a type guarantee.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the approved prefix contains orders-a.csv and orders-b.csv, while the task names orders-b.csv. Inspect the listing, select that object by name and download it to the declared local path. Read it with the declared types, then compare its columns and row count with the supplied expectation. An order key such as ‘0012’ is example data worth inspecting after conversion: its loaded representation must match the key contract. If the supplied task instead requires selected columns from a Parquet dataset, relate that choice to the declared access pattern rather than changing formats arbitrarily. Write a local text identity record inside its open-file block so the retrieval and inspection have an identifiable result.

The listing and the loaded table answer different questions. Listing confirms which objects are available under the authorized location; table inspection confirms how the chosen object's bytes were interpreted. Keep the local path in the retrieval result so a later read cannot accidentally inspect an earlier download. CSV and Parquet should be discussed in terms of the supplied access requirement: text-and-type conversion versus columnar typed access. A selected-column Parquet read does not excuse omitting a column the task needs, just as a CSV conversion does not excuse changing a key's declared representation. Verify the loaded result before calling ingestion complete.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Successful download is not evidence that the right columns or representations were loaded. Inferred types are not a type guarantee, and the existing runtime identity still governs authorized access.

teaching_blocks.title: Ingest and Inspect Model Data
teaching_blocks.content: The order dataset is larger than the permitted working array. You need a bounded stream-processing plan, not a plan that reads chunks and then keeps every chunk in a growing collection. The array budget applies to what you materialize for each working chunk.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use pd.read_csv(file_handle, chunksize=row_limit, dtype=declared_types) as an iterator of bounded row chunks, and process it with a for loop rather than retaining the entire dataset. For a homogeneous fixed-width feature matrix with F columns and element width W bytes, a chunk of R rows requires R × F × W element bytes. Choose chunksize so the chunk matrix fits the stated array budget and verify each materialized chunk; this element estimate is not a guarantee about total reader or process memory.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the dataset stream open using a with open(...) block while iterating its chunks.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Assume the declared feature matrix has 20 columns of eight-byte elements and an array budget of 16,000 bytes. A 100-row chunk uses 100 × 20 × 8 = 16,000 element bytes. A 101-row chunk would use 16,160 bytes and fail that particular bound. Keep the file open while iterating the reader, process one chunk, and verify each materialized matrix rather than inferring its size only from the reader setting. The final chunk may contain fewer rows; apply the same bound to it. This example accounts for the homogeneous feature matrix only. It does not establish a bound on parsing buffers, other objects or the process as a whole.

Treat the arithmetic as a per-chunk admission check. The reader setting proposes an upper row count, but the working matrix's actual shape and dtype determine its element bytes. The final short chunk remains a valid chunk rather than a reason to invent padding rows. Process and emit or summarize that chunk within the declared bounded workflow, then continue without accumulating prior chunks into a full dataset. If the feature width changes, recompute the bound from the actual column count; the old 100-row estimate no longer establishes the same storage requirement. The open file context must encompass the whole iteration, not end before the reader finishes.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A chunksize is not a total-memory guarantee. The element calculation is a bounded allocation estimate, and retaining all processed chunks would defeat the intended working-chunk approach.

teaching_blocks.title: Ingest and Inspect Model Data
teaching_blocks.content: Before transforming order data, produce a readiness record another caller can inspect. A single ‘looks fine’ conclusion hides whether you checked columns, numerical axes or feasible element storage. Named results make the same inspection questions repeatable.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect the loaded dataset column names, dtypes and descriptive summaries before declaring it ready for model input. Report the feature matrix shape and dtype, retaining the meaning of each axis rather than only the total number of elements. Report matrix element memory with array.nbytes and distinguish it from total process memory.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Return named readiness results as a dictionary from a parameterized inspection function, so callers can check the same fields. Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values, axis=0), so each selected numeric feature column is summarized over rows. Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, axis=0, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Use a two-column fixture with rows [2, 10], [4, 20] and [6, 30]. Its feature shape is (3, 2): three observations, two features. The column means are 4 and 20. With the population divisor, the first column's standard deviation is the square root of 8/3, about 1.633. Record the dtype and array.nbytes as observed, together with column names and summaries. Return those results in a dictionary from a function whose input and inspection choices are explicit parameters. Another caller should be able to inspect the same named fields for a different fixture rather than parse a paragraph or rely on values left in an interactive session. Keep the two axis meanings alongside their lengths.

The dictionary should make the observation count and feature count directly accessible under their own names. A caller inspecting a width mismatch should not need to infer it from the means. Likewise, record units or the selected numerical observations beside summaries so a feature's mean is not confused with an average over every number in the matrix. Computing feature-wise summaries over the observation axis produces one result per feature. Keep dtype and element bytes as observed representation properties, distinct from the task's value summaries. A readiness verdict can then be traced to named evidence rather than to an opaque statement that the data was inspected.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A dataset's total element count is not a readiness summary. Standard deviation also depends on the specified divisor: ddof=0 and a calculation requiring ddof=1 are not interchangeable.

teaching_blocks.title: Validate and Clean Datasets
teaching_blocks.content: Your declared dataset has distance and zone fields, with permitted types and value ranges. A table can load successfully while missing zone or containing a distance outside its contract. Schema validation turns those expectations into explicit acceptance checks.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A dataset schema declares expected features and their permitted representations or values; absent, unexpected or invalid features are schema violations. Compare table.columns and table.dtypes with the declared column/type contract before checking each constrained column. Implement value constraints as boolean predicates and raise an explicit validation exception when a required column, type or value boundary fails.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this invented contract, distance must be numeric and between 0 and 100 inclusive; zone must use the declared representation. A row at distance 0 exercises the lower boundary, while −1 is a failure fixture. A table with an unexpected third feature fails the stated column contract even if all its values look plausible. Compare the column set and types first, then evaluate each constrained column with boolean predicates. Use an explicit validation exception when a required condition fails. Keep fixtures for a valid table, a permitted boundary and a failed condition, so a later change does not quietly alter what the contract accepts. The checks concern the declared schema, not guesses about what a downstream model might tolerate.

Separate a column-contract failure from a value-contract failure. A missing zone field prevents the declared table schema from being satisfied; a present zone field with an invalid representation is a different reason to reject. The numerical limit test also needs its stated inclusive boundary rather than an assumed strict inequality. Write the failure so the caller can identify the violated condition without guessing from a later estimator exception. Replaying both valid and rejected fixtures verifies that the validator is neither accepting everything nor rejecting everything. Its purpose is to enforce the supplied contract before downstream work depends on that contract.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Loading a table does not validate it. Assertions exercise the fixtures in ordinary non-optimized execution; explicit exceptions enforce rejection of invalid input in the declared validation path.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: A schema is an executable contract for admissible dataset structure.

teaching_blocks.title: Validate and Clean Datasets
teaching_blocks.content: An order appears twice, and another has an invalid distance. Cleaning should follow the supplied retain, repair or reject policy, not an engineer's unrecorded preference. The important result includes what happened to the affected observations.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use a set of accepted observation keys to test whether a key has already been seen before adding the next accepted key. Use a policy dictionary to choose the declared retain, repair or reject action for each detected invalid or repeated observation. Inspect and clean example data as needed, making representations consistent with its intended training use.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Implement the declared action with conditional branches and report the affected observation IDs, instead of silently altering the dataset. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the approved policy retains the first accepted order key, rejects a repeated accepted key, and repairs a specified zone spelling. Start with an empty accepted-key set. After accepting order A, add A; when A appears again, detect the repeat before accepting it. Apply the policy dictionary's action through explicit branches and record A as affected. For order B with the approved spelling issue, record the repair and its ID. A different defect may require rejection rather than that same repair. Test a valid observation, the declared boundary and a repeated-key fixture. This example does not choose a universal deduplication rule: it implements the rule supplied for this dataset and its intended training use.

A useful cleaning report lets a reviewer trace each affected ID back to the applied policy action. Do not combine ‘repaired’ and ‘rejected’ into an undifferentiated issue count: a repaired record contributes different resulting data from a rejected record. Membership in the accepted-key set is also about the accepted observation history, so follow the supplied action order rather than adding every seen key indiscriminately. The repaired fixture should have its expected resulting values checked, while the duplicate fixture should verify that the prohibited repeat was not accepted. Retain valid observations according to the same policy; defect handling should not replace the dataset's stated purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Cleaning is not permission to silently rewrite observations. A duplicate or invalid record needs its declared action and affected ID reported; the policy decides the action, not merely the presence of a defect.

teaching_blocks.title: Representation, Labels and Splits
teaching_blocks.content: Your collected order sample contains few observations from one delivery zone. Before treating its summary as a picture of the intended prediction population, compare what was included with the supplied target-population counts.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Data omitted by collection or filtering can exclude observations that matter to the intended prediction population. Compare each category count divided by its population total between the supplied sample and target population to identify supported coverage differences. For a category with known target membership, estimate inclusion probability as included category members divided by all target category members; an empty denominator cannot support a rate.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Unequal sampling probabilities affect the interpretation of a sample; a descriptive sample summary is not automatically representative of the target population. Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values) over the selected numeric observations. Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the target population has 60 zone-A orders and 40 zone-B orders, while the sample includes 30 A and 10 B. Target proportions are 0.60 and 0.40; sample proportions are 0.75 and 0.25. With known membership, estimated inclusion probabilities are 30/60 = 0.50 for A and 10/40 = 0.25 for B. These calculations show a supported coverage difference and unequal inclusion. They do not establish that every characteristic of either zone differs. You can also summarize a selected numerical feature with its mean and standard deviation, retaining the specified observations and divisor. If a category has no target members in the supplied denominator, do not manufacture an inclusion rate for it.

Read the ratios as separate conditional questions. The sample's 0.75 zone-A share asks which zone an included observation belongs to. The 0.50 zone-A inclusion probability asks whether a target-population zone-A observation was included. Neither is the target's 0.60 zone-A share. Naming the numerator and denominator in the record prevents a later user from interpreting a selection statistic as population prevalence. The numerical summaries are descriptive evidence for the selected values only. The supported limitation is unequal observed coverage under these supplied counts, not a claim that a particular model must fail or that an unobserved cause of selection has been established.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A descriptive sample statistic is not automatically a target-population statistic. Keep sample totals, target totals and inclusion denominators distinct instead of treating all three ratios as the same quantity.

video_need.reason: Aligned sample and population counts make coverage and inclusion denominators easier to distinguish.

teaching_blocks.content: The labels arrive in a different order from the observations. Joining the first label to the first row would give an apparently complete dataset without establishing that each target belongs to the right example. Use the intended observation identity.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A label must match its prediction or observation through the intended unique identifier, rather than through incidental row order. Check for repeated IDs before building an ID-to-label dictionary, because assigning an existing dictionary key replaces its earlier value. Use set differences between observation IDs and label IDs to detect observations missing labels and labels with no observation.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Use keyed dictionary lookups to compare each label, observation timestamp and availability timestamp against the task-specific acceptance predicates. Do not treat information unavailable at the relevant prediction boundary as an available input to that prediction. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Let observations have IDs A and B, while the label file lists B then A. A keyed lookup attaches each label to its own observation despite the reversed order. Before constructing the label dictionary, check repeated IDs: two labels for A would otherwise compete for the same dictionary key. Compare observation and label ID sets to reveal a missing label or a label without an observation. Then inspect the matched timestamps under the supplied acceptance predicates. A label's later availability does not turn it into an input available at the earlier prediction time. Exercise reordered, duplicate, missing and declared boundary fixtures so correct row counts do not conceal incorrect correspondence.

Construct the observation-ID and label-ID sets before declaring the join complete. Their differences identify the two unmatched directions: observations without labels and labels without observations. Duplicate IDs need handling before a dictionary silently replaces a value, because set equality alone would not reveal two label rows with the same ID. After the keyed join, inspect the supplied timestamp boundary on the matched record. Key correspondence and time suitability are independent requirements: a correctly keyed label can still be unsuitable under a stated time predicate. This order of checks produces aligned, permitted examples rather than an apparently complete table whose targets belong to another row.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Matching row counts is not matching identities. A dictionary assignment replaces an existing key's value, so building the dictionary first can hide a duplicate that should have been handled explicitly.

teaching_blocks.title: Representation, Labels and Splits
teaching_blocks.content: The intended evaluation asks how the system behaves on later orders or on groups absent from training. A random division is not automatically the right simulation. Choose and test the boundary supplied for that deployment scenario.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A random split is appropriate only if its sampling interpretation matches the intended evaluation; dependent grouped or time-ordered data can require different boundaries. Keep observations from a common evaluation group entirely on one side of the boundary, and keep time-ordered training observations earlier than the intended later evaluation observations. Implement the supplied group membership with sets and assert that training and validation group intersections are empty.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For a time boundary, select training observations before the cutoff and later evaluation observations under the stated scenario, and check the timestamp inequalities. Calculate each partition’s target outcome count divided by its partition total to report the population actually evaluated. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a group-based fixture, suppose orders A and B belong to customer G1, while C belongs to G2. Keeping G1 wholly in training and G2 wholly in validation satisfies that group boundary; putting A in training and B in validation does not. Assert that the group-set intersection is empty. For a separate time-boundary fixture, use training observations before the cutoff and evaluation observations in the declared later interval, checking the inequalities directly. Report the target proportion within each partition: if validation contains four target events among ten examples, its proportion is 0.40. That number describes the cohort actually evaluated, not automatically the whole intended population. Keep group and time scenarios tied to their respective supplied evaluation interpretation.

The set-intersection assertion asks whether the same group identity appears on both sides, not whether two individual order IDs repeat. Distinct observations from G1 can still violate a group boundary. In the time fixture, compare timestamp extrema or the supplied inequalities under the stated cutoff; distinct group sets do not establish temporal ordering. Reporting each partition's target prevalence helps describe what the evaluation cohort actually contains, but it does not choose the boundary retrospectively. Fix the deployment-matched interpretation first, assign observations accordingly and then inspect whether the resulting partitions satisfy it. The evaluation claim must stay tied to that simulated scenario.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Random is not a synonym for deployment-matched. Group dependence or time ordering can require a different boundary, and an empty group intersection does not by itself test timestamp ordering.

teaching_blocks.title: Fit and Compose Preprocessing
teaching_blocks.content: An order feature is missing in some rows. A replacement learned from training is part of the fitted representation; it should not change just because validation contains a different mix of values. Separate learning the replacement from applying it.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: SimpleImputer learns one replacement value per feature from the data passed to fit, with strategies including mean, median, most_frequent and constant. Use SimpleImputer(strategy=declared_strategy).fit(X_train), then call transform(X_validation) without fitting on validation rows. Inspect statistics_ to check the fitted replacement values and verify they remain unchanged after validation transformation.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values, axis=0), so each selected numeric feature column is summarized over rows. Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, axis=0, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the observed training distances are 2 and 6, and the declared strategy is mean. Their mean is 4, so the fitted replacement for a missing distance is 4. If validation contains distance 100 and a missing value, transform it using the stored replacement rather than incorporating 100 into a new mean. Inspect statistics_ before and after transformation to confirm the replacement stayed fixed. Keep checks for a complete row, a missing row and the declared boundary case. If the readiness calculation also asks for feature spread, use the specified standard-deviation divisor on the selected numerical observations; that summary is distinct from selecting the imputer strategy. Other supplied strategies may call for a different replacement, so do not treat this example's mean as a general requirement.

The missing validation row is an application case for the stored statistic. It is not an extra observation from which to relearn the statistic, and the observed value 100 belongs to the held-out cohort rather than the training reference. Check the transformed result and statistics_ together: the expected replacement verifies the output, while unchanged statistics verify reuse of the fitted state. This distinction remains important if the supplied strategy is median, most_frequent or constant instead of mean. The chosen strategy defines how the replacement is learned or supplied; the train-versus-transform boundary defines when its state may change. Preserve both choices in the bounded workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Calling fit on validation learns a different state. Transforming validation is reuse of the training state, not a request to choose a replacement that looks more suitable for the held-out rows.

teaching_blocks.title: Fit and Compose Preprocessing
teaching_blocks.content: Training and validation orders have different distance ranges. Scaling should put both through the same fitted rule, not make each cohort define its own reference. The training mean and scale are the state you inspect and reuse.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: StandardScaler centers each feature using its training mean and scales by its training standard deviation when with_mean and with_std are enabled. Fit StandardScaler on X_train and reuse its transform on X_validation; mean_ and scale_ expose the stored training parameters. A constant feature cannot be scaled to unit variance, so StandardScaler leaves its scaling factor as 1.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Validation and prediction inputs must receive the transformations used for training, rather than separately fitted transformations. Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values, axis=0), so each selected numeric feature column is summarized over rows. Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, axis=0, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.content: Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Take a training feature with values 2 and 6. Its mean is 4 and its population standard deviation is 2. With centering and scaling enabled, those values become −1 and 1. A validation value of 8 becomes (8−4)/2 = 2 under the stored training rule. Separately fitting validation would no longer apply that rule. Inspect mean_ and scale_ and check that validation transformation does not replace them. Include a constant-feature fixture: the scaler uses a scaling factor of 1 rather than turning a constant feature into unit variance. Record feature-wise summaries over rows with the specified divisor so the reference calculation and the fitted parameter interpretation remain aligned.

A validation value beyond the training range can legitimately receive a transformed value beyond the training fixture's transformed values. The value 2 for validation distance 8 follows the fixed formula; it is not a reason to refit until validation has its own mean zero. Verify the column-wise mean and population spread used in the hand calculation, then inspect the fitted parameters corresponding to that feature. Centering and scaling configuration also matters: the stated formula assumes both are enabled. For a constant training feature, report the factor of 1 and the resulting behavior rather than describing an impossible unit-variance transformation. All later cohorts reuse this same fitted interpretation.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Scaling is not ‘make every incoming dataset have its own zero mean.’ Validation and prediction reuse training transformations; a constant feature cannot be forced to unit variance by that scaler.

teaching_blocks.title: Fit and Compose Preprocessing
teaching_blocks.content: An order's zone is a category rather than a numerical distance. The fitted category mapping determines the indicator columns. Before accepting held-out rows, make explicit what happens to a category the training fit never encountered.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: OneHotEncoder learns categories from fit data and represents each categorical value with the corresponding indicator columns. Fit the encoder on the training categories, inspect categories_, and use transform for validation inputs without relearning the mapping. Choose handle_unknown explicitly: its default error rejects unknown categories, whereas ignore produces all-zero indicators for an unknown category in that feature.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Missing categorical values can be represented as a learned category when present at fit time; missing values absent from the learned categories follow the unknown-category behavior. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution. Build the training-category dictionary from the fitted encoder’s categories_ and feature names, and keep list-based known, unseen and missing cases aligned with that stored mapping.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose training contains north and south. Inspect categories_ and store the category dictionary with the feature name, using the fitted order rather than inventing a new one. Under a two-column north/south mapping, a known north row has its corresponding indicator set. An unseen east row is rejected by the default error policy; with handle_unknown set to ignore, it has all-zero indicators for that feature. Keep known, unseen and missing fixtures aligned with the stored mapping. Missing values present during fit can become a learned category; missing values absent from the learned set follow the unknown-category behavior. That distinction means two missing-value fixtures may need different expectations depending on what the fit actually saw.

The output width depends on the fitted category set, not on the number of categories occurring in a particular validation batch. Keep columns aligned to the stored training mapping even if a batch contains only north. An unseen east fixture tests the explicit policy without silently extending categories_ during transformation. For the missing fixture, first ask whether missing was represented in the fit data. If yes, its learned indicator follows that mapping; if not, it follows the unknown-category rule. These checks distinguish stable column identity from changing observed batch contents. The metadata dictionary records that identity so the representation remains interpretable to downstream callers.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: An all-zero unknown indicator does not mean the encoder learned an ‘east’ category. Also, missing and unseen are not universally identical: the fit data and explicit unknown policy determine their treatment.

teaching_blocks.title: Fit and Compose Preprocessing
teaching_blocks.content: Your order dataset needs one operation for numerical columns and another for zones before the estimator receives inputs. A fitted pipeline keeps those declared transformations attached to the prediction path instead of asking each caller to recreate them.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Construct Pipeline([(name, transformer), ..., (name, estimator)]) to chain transformations with a final estimator. Pipeline.fit fits the transformations and final estimator on training data, while predict applies the fitted transformations before prediction. ColumnTransformer applies declared transformers to selected columns, so categorical and numerical columns can use different operations within the same fitted workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Reuse that fitted pipeline for validation and bounded inference rather than fitting a new preprocessing state. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Imagine distance uses the declared numerical transformer while zone uses the fitted category encoder. ColumnTransformer assigns those operations to their named columns. Pipeline chains the resulting transformation with the final estimator. Fit that workflow on training data, then predict validation through the same fitted object. A fixture should check the expected transformed representation and final output for a valid input, and the supplied boundary and failure cases. If an engineer manually prepares validation with a new encoder, it no longer follows this workflow even if the estimator object is unchanged. Trace one row from selected columns through transformations to the estimator so the distinction between fitting the workflow and applying it is visible.

Trace a complete prediction call rather than testing transformations and estimation as unrelated pieces. The incoming raw columns are selected, their fitted operations are applied and the resulting representation reaches the final estimator. Intermediate pipeline steps must support fitting and transformation; the final step is the estimator. A manually prepared validation array can accidentally skip a step or use a newly learned category order, which is why the fixture should exercise the fitted workflow's own prediction path. Preserve column assignment and fitted state together. Successful estimation of an already transformed array is not evidence that the raw-input pipeline handles the declared contract correctly.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A pipeline is not a reason to refit for every cohort. Its predict path applies fitted transformations; changing preprocessing state changes the representation presented to the final estimator.

teaching_blocks.title: Prevent Prediction-Time Leakage
teaching_blocks.content: A validation result looks unusually strong, but an order's eventual arrival has reached the features. The question is not just whether the evaluation rows were held out. Audit what information reached fitting and what was available for each prediction.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Leakage uses information not available at prediction time when building a model and can make held-out performance estimates overly optimistic. Audit which rows and fields reach fit operations and each prediction, then remove held-out or future information from those operations. Separate training and evaluation before fitting preprocessing, and call transform rather than fit or fit_transform on held-out inputs.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For predictions made at acceptance, a field populated only after arrival is unavailable at the required boundary. Remove it from the prediction input rather than describing the strong held-out result as reliable evidence for this task. Also trace the preprocessing fit: if it saw both training and validation rows, separating the estimator's fit alone did not keep held-out information out of the fitted system. Split before fitting preprocessing and apply transform to held-out inputs. In the bounded fixture, retain explicit checks that no future field enters the prediction and that the fit receives only the designated training rows. The audit is about information flow, not merely whether files have different names.

Distinguish the prediction-time audit from the held-out-fit audit. The former asks whether each input field could have been known at the declared decision time. The latter asks whether any fitted choice used held-out observations. Removing the eventual-arrival feature addresses the first issue but does not repair a scaler already fitted on validation; splitting before fit addresses the second but does not make a future field available at acceptance. Test both information paths in the bounded fixture. The corrected workflow should produce held-out predictions from training-fitted state and decision-available inputs, not merely show a lower score after deleting a suspicious column.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A held-out label file does not guarantee leakage-free evaluation. Future fields and held-out rows reaching preprocessing fits can both violate the intended boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: Prevent Prediction-Time Leakage
teaching_blocks.content: You are constructing a feature from an order's earlier records. Some records were added after the prediction was made, and a lookup table has changed since then. Build the feature from the recorded availability boundary rather than today's complete view.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A feature for a prediction must be derived only from information available when that prediction is made. A list comprehension of the form [row for row in records if row["available_at"] <= prediction_time] selects the records available at the declared boundary. A changing lookup table can yield different training and serving values, so use values from the relevant recorded boundary rather than assuming the latest table is historical.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Test the feature on the original records and on records augmented with later unavailable observations, asserting that the earlier feature is unchanged. Apply the declared arithmetic feature to the time-filtered records only; for a sum, initialize total = 0 and accumulate total += record["value"] over the accepted list.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose an order has available records with values 2 and 3 at the decision time, plus a later record with value 7. For the declared sum feature, filter by available_at first, initialize the total to zero, and accumulate only the accepted values. The earlier feature is 5, not 12. Add the later record to the test input and assert that the earlier feature remains 5. If the feature also uses a changing lookup value, retrieve the value appropriate to the recorded boundary instead of treating the current lookup as historical. This test checks the feature computation's response to later information; it does not require later records to be deleted from the source system.

Preserve the calculation's order in the code and the test: inspect availability, decide membership, then update the accumulator. Summing every record and later removing a timestamp field would not remove the later record's contribution. Adding the value 7 is a useful invariance test because the earlier prediction boundary has not changed. The historical lookup check is the corresponding question for changing reference state. Both mechanisms enforce the same declared availability boundary, but they concern different inputs to the feature. Retain a boundary fixture for a record at the exact permitted time under the supplied predicate instead of assuming whether equality is included.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A timestamp in the source is not enough if the calculation ignores it. The availability filter must precede the arithmetic, and a latest lookup value is not automatically the value available at an earlier prediction.

teaching_blocks.title: Protect Sensitive ML Assets
teaching_blocks.content: An inspection record contains useful diagnostics and a credential. The dataset or log being readable does not grant permission to redistribute every field. Apply the existing identity and permitted-field policy before creating a new record.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Data access is governed by authenticated identities and authorization, not merely by possession of a dataset or log file. Implement the supplied permitted-field policy with dictionary membership checks and create a record containing only the permitted values. Credentials written into an image or its metadata can be exposed; remove literal credentials from the data/log sample rather than treating them as ordinary diagnostic values.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the credential value in the authorized runtime secret mechanism rather than copying it into a generated record.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied policy permits run_id and row_count, but not token or raw customer values. Construct a dictionary containing the permitted fields using membership checks; the new record should contain the run identifier and count without the credential. Keep the credential in the authorized runtime secret mechanism, not in an image, metadata or diagnostic record. Test a sample containing both permitted and forbidden keys and inspect the resulting record rather than assuming a field was removed. This is implementation of an existing policy, not permission to invent new readers or expand the permitted field list. A useful error report can identify the handling problem without reproducing the literal credential.

Build a new permitted-field dictionary rather than copying the whole input and hoping no forbidden field remains. The membership rule should use the existing allowed-field collection; adding a field because it appears diagnostically useful would change policy. Inspect both the returned dictionary and the captured output. A removed token field in the returned record does not establish non-disclosure if the input was printed beforehand. Runtime credential delivery and diagnostic-field selection address related but distinct handling paths. Keep the credential reference usable by the permitted runtime while keeping its literal value absent from generated data, metadata, images and logs.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Possession of a file is not authorization to expose its contents. Moving a literal credential from a data sample into image metadata or a generated diagnostic record does not remove the exposure risk.

teaching_blocks.title: Metrics and Acceptance Criteria
teaching_blocks.content: A late-order classifier can make few total mistakes while missing many of the orders the team wanted to catch. Select a metric whose conditioning population and error consequences match the task, rather than treating a single accuracy value as the whole answer.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Select classification metrics in relation to task consequences, class balance and the costs of false positives and false negatives, rather than relying on raw accuracy alone. Precision = TP/(TP+FP) is the proportion of predicted positives that are actual positives, while recall = TP/(TP+FN) is the proportion of actual positives detected. For regression, mean absolute error averages absolute prediction errors and mean squared error averages squared errors; the latter increases the influence of large errors.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Class prevalence is the proportion of actual positives in the validation population and helps interpret metrics from that population. Conditional frequencies from a validation confusion table describe outcomes in that cohort; they do not establish that a model’s individual probability scores are calibrated.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Consider TP=12, FP=3, FN=8 and TN=77. Precision is 12/(12+3) = 0.80: among predicted positives, four in five are actual positives. Recall is 12/(12+8) = 0.60: among actual positives, three in five are detected. Prevalence is 20/100 = 0.20 in this validation cohort. For a separate regression task, errors of 1 and 3 give MAE 2 and MSE 5; the squared-error average gives the larger error more influence. Keep the task's false-positive and false-negative consequences beside these quantities. The confusion-table ratios summarize outcomes in this cohort; they do not establish that an individual score such as 0.8 is calibrated.

Walk the confusion table by the question being asked. Precision starts from the predicted-positive group of 15; recall starts from the actual-positive group of 20. FPR instead starts from the actual-negative group, while FNR starts from actual positives. Attaching the relevant counts to a ratio makes it harder to swap these populations. For regression, the same two residuals give different MAE and MSE because squaring changes the aggregation. Choose the declared metric according to target type and error consequences before comparing results. None of these aggregate outcome summaries establishes that individual probability scores match observed outcome frequencies at each score value.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Precision and recall condition on different groups. Neither can be substituted for the other, and cohort frequencies are not proof of probability-score calibration.

teaching_blocks.title: Track and Tune Reproducibly
teaching_blocks.content: Candidate results vary across repeated trials. Control the supplied random sources and compare paired results, while keeping the trial count visible. This is evidence about the declared repeated comparison, not a guarantee of universal determinism.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Integer random_state values reset supported scikit-learn random generators for repeatable calls, while None or a shared RandomState instance has different state-consumption behavior. Control the estimator and split random sources for a comparison, but distinguish that control from a guarantee that every computation or environment is deterministic. Use a for loop over the declared seed list to execute the repeated comparison and collect each matched pair of validation results.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Estimate the candidate’s empirical win probability as winning paired trials divided by all completed paired trials, retaining the number of trials. Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values) over the selected numeric observations. Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the declared seed list yields five completed matched baseline/candidate pairs and the candidate wins three. Its empirical win probability is 3/5 = 0.60 for those trials. Record each pair, not just separate averages that lose the pairing. Compute the mean and specified standard deviation over the selected results, retaining the population or sample-divisor interpretation. Supported integer random_state settings reset generators for repeatable calls, but None or a shared RandomState has different state consumption. Control both estimator and split sources as required. If a trial is not completed, do not silently count it as a win; keep the completed-pair denominator explicit.

Retain the trial's seed and baseline/candidate results in the same record so the win calculation can be reconstructed pair by pair. A mean over candidate results and a separate mean over baseline results may summarize levels, but it does not retain which matched trials were wins. The supplied seed protocol also governs splits where applicable, not only the estimator. Report the empirical 0.60 alongside the five completed pairs and the declared spread calculation. This bounded evidence supports a repeatability comparison while leaving unsupported environmental or computation-wide determinism claims unresolved.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A controlled seed does not guarantee that every environment or computation is deterministic. A three-in-five empirical win result also describes these completed trials, not certainty that the candidate always wins.

teaching_blocks.content: The order model fits training well but performs worse on validation under the same score interpretation. That gap supports investigating overfitting. teaching_blocks.title: The working rule

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:

The validation comparison remains fixed as you vary the supplied regularization setting. Do not quietly change cost assumptions, cohorts or a different estimator parameter at the same time. A training/validation gap under comparable score definitions is evidence about generalization worth investigating; the chosen setting is selected from its validation evidence and required limits. Keep estimator names beside alpha or C so their opposite penalty-direction interpretations are unambiguous. The protected-test boundary applies to regularization just as it does to model choice. A final test result cannot become an extra trial in this tuning comparison.

teaching_blocks.title: Document Model Risks
teaching_blocks.content: The model's risk record must describe its permitted identities and supported task limitations. It should not expand policy or reproduce a secret merely to document that the secret was exposed.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Compare supplied access grants against the existing policy’s permitted identity scope, recording any grant outside that scope rather than defining a new authorization policy. Literal credentials in an image or its metadata are an exposure risk, so a risk record should describe the handling limitation without copying the secret value. Model performance can differ by segment even when the aggregate result improves; state the supported limitations of the supplied evaluation rather than implying universal suitability.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Build the single record from the existing policy fields, preserving the supplied permitted identities, documented task limits and foreseeable misuse cases without extending the permission scope.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied policy permits identity A but the inspected grant list also includes B. Record B as outside the permitted scope; do not add B to the policy to make the audit pass. If a sample image contains a literal credential, describe the handling limitation without copying that value. Include the documented task limits, foreseeable misuse cases and supported segment limitations from the supplied records. A better aggregate validation result does not justify wording that implies every segment is suitable. Build one record preserving the existing policy fields, so a reader can distinguish permitted use, an observed access mismatch and a supported evaluation limitation.

Use policy language for permissions and evidence language for limitations. An observed grant mismatch is compared with the allowed identity set; it is not repaired by expanding that set in the documentation. A supported segment limitation belongs to the evaluation record and should be described at that scope. A credential-handling issue can be identified through the field or location concerned without reproducing the value. Preserve the task's foreseeable misuse cases and stated permitted use alongside the observed facts. This separation prevents the record from becoming either a new authorization policy or an unsupported claim of suitability.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep

teaching_blocks.title: Tensors, Minibatches and Model Outputs
teaching_blocks.content: The numerical order arrays must become aligned PyTorch inputs. Feature and target representation are separate parts of the contract; converting both to whichever dtype the features happen to have is not a sufficient check.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use import torch and torch.from_numpy(array) to construct tensors from the supplied NumPy feature and target arrays. Convert the feature and target tensors explicitly with tensor.to(dtype=declared_dtype), inspect tensor.shape and tensor.dtype, and verify row correspondence rather than relying on inferred types or deriving target representation from feature dtype. Assert the declared feature and target axis lengths and their common batch length, and return the aligned tensors as a tuple.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose features have shape (4, 2), and the declared targets have shape (4,). Construct tensors from the two NumPy arrays, explicitly convert each to its declared dtype, and inspect the resulting shapes and dtypes. Return the aligned pair as a tuple only after checking the common batch length and required axes. A target fixture with three rows fails correspondence even if each target value is individually permitted. Another fixture can test an incorrect declared target representation without changing the feature dtype. Keeping these checks separate makes it clear whether a failure concerns feature shape, target shape, dtype or matching observations, rather than reporting only that conversion succeeded.

Inspect features and targets separately before checking their common observation axis. A classification target representation may differ from numerical features, so an explicit cast should use the target's declared dtype rather than a shared convenience setting. Return the pair only after the axes and representations satisfy the contract. In the three-target failure fixture, tensor conversion may still succeed; the alignment check is what rejects it. Test that failure alongside an accepted pair and the supplied boundary. This establishes a reliable input contract for later minibatch use without relying on a subsequent loss to expose an earlier conversion error.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A map-style Dataset implements __len__ for sample count and __getitem__(index) for the corresponding feature/target item. Construct DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=declared_size, shuffle=declared_order_policy) and iterate for features, targets in loader.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: The loader groups observation items into minibatches while preserving the feature/target relationship within each item. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For five indexed observations and batch_size 2, a fixture with drop_last=False retains batches of sizes 2, 2 and 1. With drop_last=True, it retains two complete batches and discards the incomplete final batch. Retrieve each feature and target from the same observation index in __getitem__, and return them together. Test the batch boundaries and observed pairings under the declared shuffle policy rather than assuming a loader output's first position still corresponds to the source's first row. Also check __len__ against the sample count. The choice about the incomplete batch must appear in the fixture expectations, because counting three batches of size two would invent an observation.

Indexing defines correspondence before batching. If __getitem__ uses the feature at one index and the target at another, a loader can still collate a well-shaped but incorrectly paired batch. Test item identities as well as batch dimensions. The five-observation fixture also exposes the final partial-batch policy: retaining it gives one smaller batch, while dropping it changes how much of the dataset is consumed. Shuffle governs order, not whether a feature and its target remain the same item. Keep these responsibilities distinct so the expected loader output is tied to the dataset contract rather than assumed from its shape alone.

teaching_blocks.content: A minibatch loader does not make a partial batch full. Dropping or retaining the final incomplete batch is an explicit policy, and feature/target alignment begins with the dataset item.

teaching_blocks.title: Gradients, Loss and Optimizer
teaching_blocks.content: A scalar loss must send the intended learning signal through the linear computation to its parameters. Autograd's result is inspectable: compare parameter gradients with a matrix-shaped chain-rule reference, not just with an expectation that backward should work.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Autograd records tensor operations as a computation graph and differentiates the scalar output through that graph using the chain rule. Set requires_grad=True on trainable leaf tensors, form the supplied scalar loss, call loss.backward(), and inspect each leaf parameter’s .grad. Backward accumulates into .grad, so clear old gradients before comparing a fresh computation with the reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D. Compare the computed gradients to the matrix-shaped chain-rule reference with explicit relative and absolute tolerances. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Take X=[[1, 2], [3, 4]] and the supplied derivative D=[[0.1], [0.2]] for Z=XW+b. The weight-gradient reference is X.T @ D = [[0.7], [1.0]], and the bias-gradient reference is [0.3]. Any loss reduction is already included in D; dividing again would change the reference. Set trainable leaf tensors to require gradients, form the scalar loss and call backward. Inspect .grad before clearing it, and compare shapes and values under explicit tolerances. For a fresh computation, clear the old gradients first because backward accumulates. Include a failure fixture whose gradient differs from the declared reference, not only a successful call.

Read the matrix reference one parameter at a time. The first weight combines feature values 1 and 3 with derivatives 0.1 and 0.2, giving 0.7. The second combines 2 and 4 with the same derivatives, giving 1.0. The bias combines derivatives over rows, giving 0.3. These shapes are part of the check: a transpose error can yield a different object even when some scalar values look plausible. Because D includes the loss reduction, use it once as supplied. Compare after backward and before clearing so the inspected gradients correspond to the intended fresh computation rather than zeroed or accumulated state.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Backward does not overwrite every old gradient automatically. A gradient comparison also needs the correct matrix shapes and reduction convention; a numerically plausible scalar is not the weight matrix reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Gradients, Loss and Optimizer
teaching_blocks.content: The model output and target must meet the selected loss's contract. A scalar loss value alone cannot tell you whether class indices, logits, probabilities and same-shaped numerical targets were used correctly.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective. CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C). MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, averages their squared elementwise differences.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs. For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target. For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For an unweighted mean squared-error fixture with outputs [2, 4] and targets [1, 2], the loss is (1²+2²)/2 = 2.5 and output derivatives are [1, 2]. For a binary-logit fixture with one logit 0 and target 1, sigmoid(0)=0.5, so the supplied mean-logit derivative is −0.5. For target 1, decreasing the logit increases loss, while increasing it decreases loss. teaching_blocks.title: Gradients, Loss and Optimizer
teaching_blocks.content: An optimizer must receive the intended trainable parameters and apply the current gradient. A one-step deterministic fixture makes the update order and learning-rate effect concrete before you rely on a longer run.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Initialize torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=declared_learning_rate) so the optimizer receives the trainable model parameters. For plain SGD without momentum, weight decay or other modifications, the parameter update is parameter_new = parameter_old − learning_rate × gradient. Clear old parameter gradients with optimizer.zero_grad(), compute loss.backward(), then call optimizer.step() to apply the current update.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For plain SGD with no momentum, weight decay or other modifications, let a parameter be 2, its current gradient 3 and learning rate 0.1. The reference new value is 2 − 0.1 × 3 = 1.7, with change −0.3. Clear old gradients, compute backward and then step. Retain the before and after values and compare their difference with the reference under declared tolerances. Initialize the optimizer with model.parameters() so it acts on the supplied trainable model parameters. A fixture that calls backward but never step would produce a gradient without this parameter update. Keep the plain-SGD restrictions visible so this arithmetic is not mistaken for the update rule of every optimizer.

Retain the current gradient separately from the observed parameter change. The former is produced by backward; the latter is produced by step acting on the parameters bound to the optimizer. A parameter change of −0.3 matches the plain-SGD reference for gradient 3 and rate 0.1, but the same number alone would not identify what happened if those inputs differed. Check before/after values and declared tolerances together. Clearing gradients before the next backward prevents previous contributions from altering the intended fresh-step reference. teaching_blocks.title: The working rule

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example

For every minibatch, zero gradients, backpropagate that batch's loss and apply the optimizer step. Collect scalar loss.item() values with batch counts, so an epoch summary does not pretend all batches contain two observations. In the deterministic plain-SGD fixture, retain the pre-step parameter and compare its observed change with −learning_rate × current_gradient under tolerance. Test the loop's supplied valid, boundary and failure cases. The repeated sequence is what links each batch to its intended current gradient, rather than using an accumulated leftover from another batch.

Loss aggregation needs the accompanying batch counts because the last one-observation batch does not contribute the same number of examples as a two-observation batch. Record each scalar with its batch size before applying the declared epoch-summary rule. The loop's nested structure is equally important: each epoch iterates its loader, and each minibatch performs the complete current-gradient update sequence. A step outside the intended minibatch position would define a different training procedure. The deterministic fixture can inspect one update within the loop, making the control flow and parameter-change evidence meet at the same minibatch.
